Call of Duty: Black Ops 6 & Black Ops 7
Recommended…?  
Playtime: 286 hours of lag, caffeine, and emotional instability

Black Ops 6
BO6 was fun.
Fun in the same way a malfunctioning carnival ride is fun — you’re screaming, you’re laughing, you’re not sure if you’re safe, but you stay on anyway.

Campaign
I didn’t mind the campaign.
But half of it felt like Treyarch accidentally turned the storyboard into a psychedelic art project.
I’m trying to shoot enemies and suddenly I’m on a full LSD trip — colours melting, walls breathing, characters talking like they’re trapped in a fever dream.

It’s also short.
Like “I sat down to play and suddenly the credits rolled” short.

Zombies
I mostly played the campaign side of Zombies.
It wasn’t bad — just not the highlight.
It felt like Treyarch said “We’ll fix this later” and then forgot.

Microtransactions
Excessive.
Every menu feels like a shopping mall.
Every skin costs more than my actual clothes.
Every time I open the store I feel like Activision is trying to sell me my own soul.

Black Ops 7
BO7 is better — but still broken in ways that make me question the entire franchise.

End‑Game Mode (Story Continuation)
End‑Game is not Zombies.
It’s a separate mode, meant to continue the story.

Except the story isn’t really there.
It’s basically:
“Here’s some missions. Go shoot things. Don’t ask questions.”

But the gameplay loop?
Not bad.
Actually kind of fun.
Simple, repeatable, and scratches that “just one more run” itch.

Zombies
Zombies itself is fine.
The real issue is the Relics system.

The Relics system feels like it was designed by:
• a cryptographer
• a tax accountant
• and a demon
working together to make sure you never understand how progression works.

Trying to get relics feels like doing paperwork in hell.

Multiplayer
There is only one mode that is consistently populated:
Nuketown.

That’s it.
The entire multiplayer experience is basically a 24/7 Nuketown addiction simulator with people bunny‑hopping like their chairs are on fire.

Network issues?
Still here.
Still awful.
Still the same ones we’ve had since BO2.
Lag spikes, rubber‑banding, packet loss — the holy trinity of Call of Duty suffering.

Microtransactions (Again)
Same problem as BO6.
Everything is monetised.
Everything is overpriced.
Everything feels like Activision is trying to see how far they can push players before someone snaps and throws their PC into the ocean.

The Part I’m Sick Of
I’m sick of paying full price for a game that could just be a DLC at this point.

Every year it’s the same formula:
5 seasons → new game → repeat.

The life‑span of each game is so short that buying cosmetics is pointless unless you play Warzone.
And Warzone sucks too.

Activision should just make ONE Call of Duty and update it.
Add story expansions.
Add new campaigns.
Add new Zombies maps.
Add new multiplayer content.
Stop pretending every yearly release is a brand‑new game when half of it is recycled assets and the other half is a store page.

This yearly release cycle is cooked.
It’s outdated.
It’s anti‑consumer.
And it’s the reason cosmetics feel worthless the moment the next game drops.

General Thoughts
I’ve played 286 hours.
Not because the games are perfect — but because they’re fun in that chaotic, broken, “I hate this game but I also love it” Call of Duty way.

But man…
I really hope MW4 is actually good.
Not “good for a CoD game”.
Not “good once they patch it in six months”.
Not “good if you ignore the bugs and the store trying to sell you a $40 skin”.

Just good.
A normal, functioning Call of Duty.
One that doesn’t require a PhD to understand its progression systems.
One that doesn’t crash when someone sneezes in multiplayer.
One that doesn’t have microtransactions in every menu like ads on a dodgy website.

Please.
Just one good CoD again.

Final Verdict
Black Ops 6:  
Fun but broken.
Campaign is short and occasionally turns into a psychedelic drug trip.
Microtransactions everywhere.

Black Ops 7:  
Better, but still plagued by relic‑system complexity, network issues, and the eternal Nuketown addiction.
End‑Game mode has no real story, but the gameplay loop is surprisingly decent.
Zombies is fine, but relics feel like tax paperwork.

286 hours played.
I enjoyed myself.
I suffered.
I questioned my life choices.

MW4, don’t let me down.

**BO7 Multiplayer: Literally Unplayable**

Imagine using a weapon you actually like — or simply using the weapons you have access to when you’re a new player — only to realize that you’re expected to grind endlessly for attachments, skins, and even Prestige.

I’ll admit this is the first Call of Duty I’ve played, and I actually had a lot of fun during the early stages. But the more I played, the more I realized just how excessive the grinding is.

You spend hours grinding to unlock weapons and attachments, only to get destroyed by some new event or Game Pass weapon that is immediately stronger or more competitive. Then you’re expected to grind all over again just to stay competitive.

This honestly feels like toxic monetization. The base game already costs a lot, and yet there’s a new Call of Duty every year, while the game constantly pushes players toward additional paid content.

I genuinely can’t imagine what the experience is like for a completely new player. You have to grind through the early game, unlock the weapons, unlock all their attachments, learn the game, and somehow compete against players who already have everything unlocked.

I don’t mind grinding. Unlocking things and working toward progression can be fun. But this is way beyond that. The progression feels deliberately slow rather than rewarding.

**My suggestion:** at the very least, double the XP gain and make that the standard progression speed. Players should be able to experiment with different weapons and actually play the game instead of spending most of their time grinding unlocks.

I enjoyed BO7 at first, but the progression system has made the multiplayer experience incredibly frustrating.

[h1]Questionable Engagement Tactics[/h1]

Call of Duty has shifted from being a premium shooter to a product built around continuous behavioral pressure. The modern structure feels less like a game purchase and more like a recurring subscription disguised as seasonal content. The base price is already high, but the battle pass and rotating cosmetic bundles create a spending cycle that encourages players to stay financially committed. Progression systems, time limited rewards, and constant resets are designed to keep players engaged through psychological pressure rather than genuine gameplay depth.

Despite repeated claims of improved safeguards, [b][u]cheating remains rampant[/u][/b]. The developer frequently promotes new detection methods and anti cheat technology, yet the in game experience shows that cheaters are still widespread and highly visible. The gap between marketing and reality raises serious questions about whether these systems are effective or simply meant to reassure paying customers.

Enforcement is equally concerning. Automated bans, limited transparency, and minimal customer support leave players vulnerable to losing access to a product they have invested significant money into. The appeal process is unclear, slow, or nonexistent, and the platform often treats legitimate players the same as actual offenders.

[h2]Key Concerns[/h2]
[b]• Monetization pressure[/b]
The cost structure resembles a subscription more than a one time purchase.
[b]• Psychological engagement tactics[/b]
Progress bars, time limited items, and seasonal resets encourage compulsive play.
[b]• [u]Rampant cheating[/u][/b]
Cheaters remain common despite repeated claims of improved safeguards.
[b]• Opaque enforcement systems[/b]
Automated bans and limited support create risk for legitimate players.
[b]• Seasonal resets[/b]
Progress loses relevance every season, pushing players toward new purchases.

An absolute masterclass in anti-consumer user interface design that turns simply launching a video game into an infuriating chore.

Originally introduced as Activision's vision for a unified, "one-stop shop" hub for the entire franchise, the Call of Duty HQ launcher stands as one of the most hated executable files on Steam. Rather than streamlining access to your purchased games, it acts as a massive, bloated barrier. Booting up a game requires opening the HQ launcher first, staring at a cluttered screen covered in seasonal battle pass advertisements and microtransaction store banners, and selecting your game mode—only for the launcher to completely shut itself down and force your PC to boot up another separate executable just to play Warzone or an older campaign. It is an uninspired, clunky time-sink that treats your gaming library like a glorified, interactive billboard.

The technical headaches caused by this ecosystem are legendary. Because the HQ forces multiple games to share overlapping code and asset files, routine title updates constantly result in file corruption, wiped graphic settings, or massive 80GB-plus downloads just to patch a hotfix for a game mode you might not even play. To make matters worse, the launcher frequently locks up, demanding a complete game restart for every minor playlist update or shader optimization pass. It creates a ridiculous double-boot cycle where you spend five to ten minutes just fighting through application restarts, menu reloads, and crashing launchers before you can step foot onto a multiplayer map.

Ultimately, the ecosystem felt less like a feature built for player convenience and more like a corporate scheme to artificially pad player "engagement time" and push storefront sales. The community pushback grew so toxic that developers eventually had to start uncoupling games from the bloated hub to let players launch them as standalone titles again. While the concept of a single Call of Duty app sounds fine on paper, the execution is a chaotic, space-hogging, menu-cluttered disaster. It remains a prime example of how bad corporate UI design can ruin the user experience before a game even starts.

Call of Duty: Warzone is a fast-paced, high-stakes battle royale that serves as a cornerstone of the competitive FPS market, heavily prioritizing twitch reflexes and complex movement mechanics. 

Pros
* Free-to-play model offers complete access to the premier battle royale experience without any upfront cost.
* Hyper-polished, ultra-fast movement mechanics like sliding, sprinting, and mounting that feel highly fluid and responsive.
* Massive variety of rotatable casual modes, limited-time community events, and smaller resurgence maps to break up the pacing.
* The Gunsmith system allows for incredibly granular weapon custom modifications to suit highly specific playstyles.
* Massive global player base ensures rapid matchmaking queue times across all hours of the day. 

Cons
* Stiff learning curve heavily dominated by veteran players utilizing aggressive, hyper-fast movement mechanics.
* Infuriatingly bloated file size requires massive amounts of hard drive space and constant, heavy updates.
* Pervasive issues with cheaters and hackers continue to plague public matchmaking lobbies.
* Aggressive in-game monetization, intrusive cosmetic advertisements, and rapid weapon meta shifts force constant level grinding.
* Heavy visual clutter and over-the-top, collaborative pop-culture player skins break the game's tactical realism. 

Call of Duty: Warzone vs. Battlefield 6 Free Version (REDSEC)
* Destruction and Campers: Warzone features static building environments with fixed cover, restricting options against building campers to risky stairs pushes or window jumps; Battlefield 6's free mode (REDSEC) features full tactical destruction, allowing players to explode new sightlines or completely collapse structures to clear out camping teams. 
* Combat and Vehicles: Warzone focuses heavily on tight, infantry-driven gunfights while maintaining strict restraints on vehicle power; REDSEC delivers chaotic, large-scale combined arms warfare, actively incorporating high-tier armored tanks, naval ships, and combat helicopters directly into the survival loop.
* Game Modes and Sandbox: Warzone centers its free framework primarily around traditional Battle Royale and Resurgence variants; REDSEC expands its free offering by packaging its Battle Royale alongside Gauntlet (a knockout-style mission mode) and providing free, unlimited access to the Portal creation sandbox. 
* Movement and Pacing: Warzone favors arcade-style twitch reflexes, aggressive sliding, and hyper-mobile solo maneuverability; REDSEC relies on a slightly more methodical, squad-oriented layout tied to functional character class roles. 
* Matchmaking and Server Performance: Warzone enjoys incredibly stable, lightning-fast queue times due to its gargantuan community size; REDSEC offers a visually breathtaking experience but can suffer from live-service desync and fluctuating regional player populations depending on the peak hours.

Call of Duty – The Philosophical Tragedy of a Player Who Never Learned to Quit

There are games you simply play.

You start them, you have some fun, maybe you win, maybe you lose, and then you close them.

And then there is Call of Duty.

Call of Duty is not just a game. It is an emotional journey. A digital battlefield where dreams are created, destroyed, and questioned. It is a place where confidence can disappear in seconds, where victories feel legendary, and where defeats feel like a personal attack from the universe itself.

It is a game that can make you feel like the greatest player alive one moment and make you question every decision you have ever made the next.

Call of Duty is not only about weapons, kills, and winning.

It is about patience.

It is about frustration.

It is about hope.

It is about the human ability to look at a defeat and say:

“One more match.”

Even when your brain is begging you to stop.

Every player knows this feeling.

You sit down, grab your controller, start the game, and tell yourself:

“Today will be different. Today I will relax. Today I will actually enjoy myself.”

A beautiful thought.

A completely unrealistic thought.

Because Call of Duty has already prepared a different experience.

The match begins.

The map loads.

The music starts.

For a few seconds, you feel unstoppable.

You feel like the main character in an action movie.

You move forward with confidence. You check your surroundings. You are focused. You are ready.

And then…

Everything ends.

A player you never even saw appears for half a second and eliminates you before your brain can understand what happened.

You sit there quietly.

You look at the screen.

And suddenly you begin asking the deepest questions of existence:

“Was that skill?”

“Was that luck?”

“Or did that person simply spend more hours in this game than most people spend sleeping?”

Call of Duty teaches lessons that no school ever could.

It teaches patience.

It teaches acceptance.

It teaches that sometimes life is unfair.

And most importantly, it teaches that your controller is probably innocent…

but sometimes it still looks suspiciously close to the edge of the desk.

The multiplayer of Call of Duty is a perfect reflection of humanity.

There are heroes.

There are strategists.

There are beginners trying their best.

And then there are players who move around the map like they have unlocked a hidden level of human evolution.

They know every corner.

Every hiding spot.

Every possible movement.

They do not play the game.

They have become part of the game.

Meanwhile, you are just trying to survive, wondering how you ended up being the target of someone’s personal training session.

But somehow…

You press:

“Play Again.”

And that is the great mystery of Call of Duty.

No matter how frustrating it becomes, something always brings you back.

Because sometimes, everything works.

That one match.

That one perfect moment.

The moment where your aim is perfect.

Your decisions are correct.

Your reactions are faster than your thoughts.

For a few minutes, you are not just a player anymore.

You are a legend.

And that is why people keep coming back.

Not because they win every game.

But because of those rare moments where everything feels perfect.

Call of Duty is built from more than victories.

It is built from memories.

The funny moments.

The unbelievable moments.

The moments where your entire team makes the worst decision possible and somehow it works.

The moments where you laugh because the situation is so ridiculous that anger is impossible.

Of course, Call of Duty has changed.

Many players remember a time when every new release felt special. Like an event. Like something everyone was waiting for.

Today, sometimes it feels like receiving a gift you already opened before.

The box is different.

The name is different.

But somewhere inside, you recognize it.

The same old friend.

Just wearing a new outfit.

And speaking of outfits…

The skins in Call of Duty deserve their own story.

Once, soldiers looked like soldiers.

Military equipment.

Camouflage.

A serious atmosphere.

Today, you can enter a realistic battlefield and suddenly fight someone who looks like they escaped from a fantasy universe.

A trained soldier with tactical equipment faces someone wearing an outfit that looks like it was created during a strange dream at 3 AM.

At some point, you stop asking:

“How did I lose?”

And start asking:

“What exactly am I fighting?”

But maybe that is the deeper meaning of Call of Duty.

Maybe it teaches us that reality is not always logical.

Sometimes the strongest person does not win.

Sometimes the smartest person does not win.

Sometimes the person with the weirdest outfit and fastest reaction wins.

Just like life.

Call of Duty is a strange mirror of human existence.

It shows our anger.

Our ambition.

Our desire to improve.

Our refusal to give up.

Because after every defeat, every bad match, and every frustrating moment, there is always a choice.

You can quit.

Or you can try again.

And most players choose to try again.

Not because they enjoy losing.

But because somewhere inside, they believe the next match could be different.

Maybe the next shot will hit.

Maybe the next game will be the perfect game.

Maybe the next victory will finally happen.

And that small amount of hope is what keeps Call of Duty alive.

Call of Duty is not perfect.

It has problems.

It has frustrating moments.

It has moments where you stare at the screen and question every decision that brought you there.

But maybe perfection is not what makes a game unforgettable.

A perfect game would eventually become normal.

But a game that makes you angry, makes you laugh, makes you celebrate, makes you suffer, and still brings you back…

That is something special.

Because the greatest enemy in Call of Duty is not the player on the other side of the map.

The greatest enemy is the voice inside your head saying:

“Just one more game.”

A voice that has destroyed countless hours of sleep and somehow still sounds convincing.

Call of Duty is not a game for people who give up easily.

It is a test of patience.

A training course in self-control.

A lesson in accepting defeat and returning stronger.

The final truth is simple:

You do not play Call of Duty because it is always fun.

You play because somewhere between the frustration and the chaos, there is a moment that makes everything worth it.

A moment where everything feels perfect.

A moment where you remember why you started.

And after every defeat, after every loss, after every moment of anger…

You pick up the controller again.

You look at the screen.

And you say:

“Okay. One more game.”

Even though everyone knows the truth:

It will never be the last game.

The humans call this a "next-generation FPS." I call it an unmitigated sensory disaster.
I only stepped onto my human’s keyboard because they were ignoring my 4:00 AM breakfast demands. Instead, I was subjected to the absolute chaos of Black Ops 7. As a creature of high refinement, I am appalled. 



The Always-Online Campaign Absurdity: My human tried to play the campaign set in the year 2035. Right as David Mason was doing something tactical, I gracefully knocked a water glass off the desk. My human tried to pause to clean it. You cannot pause the campaign. Because it is treated like a multiplayer server, the game kept running while water soaked the carpet. Horrible design 
Deceptive Laser Traps: I saw a beautiful, glowing red dot on the monitor. Naturally, I pounced to capture it. Imagine my absolute fury when I realized the laser was behind the glass, entirely uncatchable, and providing zero tactile satisfaction.
Auditory Warfare: The flashbangs are offensive. My ears rotated 180 degrees backward and stayed there. Every time a "Death Machine" ability activates, I am forced to sprint under the couch at Mach speed.
Flawed "Omnimovement": The developers brag about a cutting-edge movement system. Yet, I didn't see a single Operator successfully leap from the floor to the top of a refrigerator in one elegant bound. If you cannot climb the curtains to look down on your enemies with judgment, it is not a real tactical game.
Zero Nutritional Rewards: You get "killstreaks" and camos, but not a single mile
The Only Positive:The PC tower expels excellent exhaust heat while trying to render the city of Avalon. It is a fantastic place to sleep, assuming the human doesn't scream into their microphone when they get shot around a corner Verdict: 1/10. Save your money and go play Stray instead.
